name: AFCAT
tagline: Fly fighters or lead ground teams as a commissioned officer in the Indian Air Force.

overview.about: The Air Force Common Admission Test is conducted online by the Indian Air Force twice a year for commissioned officer entry into the Flying Branch and the Ground Duty (Technical and Non-Technical) branches. Qualified candidates attend an Air Force Selection Board (AFSB) — Dehradun, Mysuru, Gandhinagar, Varanasi or Guwahati — for a 5-day test; Flying Branch candidates also take the Computerised Pilot Selection System (CPSS).
eligibility: Indian citizens; men and women can apply

Age: Flying Branch 20–24 years; Ground Duty (Technical & Non-Technical) 20–26 years, counted on the course start date in the notification. DGCA Commercial Pilot Licence holders get relaxation up to 26 for Flying
Flying Branch: at least 50% in Mathematics and Physics at 10+2, plus a 3-year degree with at least 60% (or B.E./B.Tech. with at least 60%)
Ground Duty (Technical): 10+2 with Physics and Mathematics and a 4-year engineering degree in the listed disciplines
Ground Duty (Non-Technical): graduation with the percentage set in the notification (varies by branch)
Candidates below 25 must be unmarried at the time of commencement of the course; always check the current notification

pattern.paper: AFCAT (General Awareness, Verbal Ability, Numerical Ability, Reasoning & Military Aptitude)
pattern.note: +3 for correct, −1 for wrong, 0 for unattempted. Section split varies; recent papers have roughly GA 25, Verbal 25, Numerical 18, Reasoning 32 (unofficial)
Mechanical / Computer Science / Electrical & Electronics streams

Time and distance (trains, boats and streams)

Spatial ability — cubes, dice, dot situation, paper folding
Engineering mathematics, engineering physics, engineering drawing
Thermodynamics, IC engines, power plant engineering
Engineering mechanics, strength of materials, material science
Theory of machines, machine design/drawing, manufacturing science, industrial engineering
Aerodynamics, flight mechanics, aircraft structures, automotive engineering
Electrical engineering — network theory, machines, power systems
Telecommunication systems, antenna & wave propagation, microwave engineering, radar
Operating systems, DBMS, computer organisation & architecture

chapters.title: General Awareness: history, polity, culture & sports

cards.title: What AFCAT GA covers
cards.body: General Awareness spans history, geography, civics and polity, art and culture, sports, basic science, environment, defence and current affairs. Questions are one-liners — you either know the fact or you don't — so wide, regular revision beats deep study here.

cards.title: History and polity in one card
cards.body: Focus on the freedom struggle (1857 to 1947), major dynasties and battles, and basic polity: Fundamental Rights (Part III), Directive Principles (Part IV), Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A), President, Parliament and Supreme Court. The President is the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces.

cards.title: Classical dances and their states
points: Manipuri — Manipur; Sattriya — Assam; Kathak — North India

cards.title: Sports basics
points: Players per side: football/hockey/cricket 11, kabaddi 7, volleyball 6, basketball 5, polo 4
Durand Cup and Santosh Trophy — football
Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna — India's highest sporting honour

cards.title: Awards
cards.body: Bharat Ratna is India's highest civilian award, followed by Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri. Gallantry awards are separate: Param Vir Chakra (wartime) and Ashoka Chakra (peacetime) are the highest in their categories.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Spend 20 minutes a day on GA from one current-affairs source plus NCERT basics. Keep a running list of 'firsts' (first woman fighter pilots, first indigenous carrier, etc.) — AFCAT asks them often.

cards.q: Kuchipudi is the classical dance of:
cards.explain: Kuchipudi originated in the village of Kuchipudi in Andhra Pradesh.

cards.q: How many players does a kabaddi team have on court?
cards.explain: A kabaddi side has 7 players on court.

cards.q: The Durand Cup is associated with:
cards.explain: The Durand Cup, started in 1888, is one of the oldest football tournaments in the world.

notes.p:
The AFCAT General Awareness section mixes **history, geography, polity, economy, art and culture, sports, science, defence and current affairs**. Questions are short one-liners, and each correct answer earns +3 while a wrong one costs −1. That makes GA the fastest section to attempt — a well-prepared candidate can finish it in 10–12 minutes and bank time for numerical ability.

This chapter covers the **static** part: facts that do not change from year to year. Static GK is the most reliable investment because it is asked in every AFCAT cycle and also helps in the SSB interview.

Revise the timeline from the Harappan civilisation to Independence using NCERT, then focus on the national movement. High-yield pairs: **Jallianwala Bagh** (13 April 1919), **Dandi March** (1930), **Quit India** (8 August 1942); **Brahmo Samaj** — Raja Ram Mohan Roy; **Arya Samaj** — Dayananda Saraswati; **Panipat** battles in 1526, 1556 and 1761.

Polity: the Constitution was adopted on **26 November 1949** and came into force on **26 January 1950**. Know the six Fundamental Rights, Art 32 (constitutional remedies), Art 51A (Fundamental Duties), Art 352/356/360 (emergencies) and Art 368 (amendment). The President is the **Supreme Commander** of the Armed Forces.
**Classical dances** recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi (with their home states):
points: Bharatanatyam — Tamil Nadu; Kathakali and Mohiniyattam — Kerala
Kuchipudi — Andhra Pradesh; Odissi — Odisha; Sattriya — Assam
Folk dances: Bihu (Assam), Garba (Gujarat), Bhangra (Punjab), Lavani (Maharashtra), Ghoomar (Rajasthan)
Musicians and instruments: Ravi Shankar — sitar; Bismillah Khan — shehnai; Amjad Ali Khan — sarod; Zakir Hussain — tabla; Shivkumar Sharma — santoor; Hariprasad Chaurasia — flute
Festivals: Onam (Kerala), Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Bihu (Assam), Hornbill Festival (Nagaland)

notes.p: Sports questions are about **players per side, terms, trophies and records**.
points: Players per side: football and hockey 11, cricket 11, volleyball 6, basketball 5, kabaddi 7 on court, polo 4
Trophies: Durand Cup and Santosh Trophy — football; Ranji Trophy — cricket; Thomas Cup (men) and Uber Cup (women) — badminton; Davis Cup — tennis
Terms: checkmate — chess; googly — cricket; love and deuce — tennis; birdie — golf
Modern Olympics began in Athens, 1896; Los Angeles hosts 2028 and Brisbane 2032
Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual Olympic gold (Beijing 2008, 10 m air rifle); Neeraj Chopra won javelin gold at Tokyo 2020
National Sports Day: 29 August (birthday of Major Dhyan Chand); the top sports award is the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna

notes.p:
Civilian honours in order: **Bharat Ratna**, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri. The **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** is for cinema and the **Jnanpith Award** for literature. For each year's winners, rely on official announcements and check the latest lists close to your exam.

Revision method: make a two-column table (item | answer) for each topic and quiz yourself by covering the right column. Go through the whole static GK table once a week.

Trap: don't confuse Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh) with Kathakali (Kerala), or the Thomas Cup (men's badminton) with the Davis Cup (tennis).
Cover the right side of each pair and test yourself.
points: Constitution adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950
Durand Cup = football; Thomas Cup = men's badminton
First individual Olympic gold: Abhinav Bindra, 2008
Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian honour

chapters.title: General Awareness: science & environment

cards.title: Science basics
cards.body: Expect Class 8–10 level questions: SI units, simple machines, light and sound phenomena, acids and bases, human body, vitamins and diseases. For an Air Force exam, basic aviation physics helps: lift, drag, thrust and weight are the four forces on an aircraft in flight.

cards.title: Flight physics
cards.body: An aircraft wing (aerofoil) makes air flow faster over its curved top surface, lowering pressure there (Bernoulli's principle) and generating **lift**. Engines provide **thrust** to overcome **drag**. Mach 1 is the speed of sound; supersonic means faster than Mach 1.

cards.title: National parks and their famous species
points: Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand) — India's first national park (1936), tigers

cards.title: Environment conventions
points: Paris Agreement (2015) — limit global warming well below 2 °C

cards.title: Greenhouse effect
cards.body: Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour trap heat in the atmosphere. Some trapping keeps Earth habitable, but extra emissions from fossil fuels and deforestation cause global warming.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Pair every environment fact with a place: a convention with its city, a species with its park. Linked facts are easier to recall under exam pressure.

cards.q: The Asiatic lion is found in the wild in:
cards.explain: Gir National Park in Gujarat is the only natural home of the Asiatic lion.

cards.q: The Montreal Protocol deals with:
cards.explain: The 1987 Montreal Protocol phases out substances that damage the ozone layer.

cards.q: Lift on an aircraft wing is best explained by:
cards.explain: Faster airflow over the wing's top lowers pressure, creating upward lift (Bernoulli's principle).

notes.p:
AFCAT science is at Class 10 level. Know the **SI units** (newton for force, joule for energy, watt for power, pascal for pressure, ohm for resistance) and common instruments: barometer (atmospheric pressure), hygrometer (humidity), anemometer (wind speed), altimeter (altitude — vital in aircraft), seismograph (earthquakes), lactometer (milk purity).

Everyday phenomena: the sky looks blue because of **scattering**; a diamond sparkles because of **total internal reflection**; sound cannot travel through vacuum; and an aircraft gains lift partly because faster air over the curved upper wing surface has lower pressure (**Bernoulli's principle**).

Chemistry: pH 7 is neutral; baking soda is NaHCO₃; rusting needs water and oxygen; CNG is mostly methane.
Biology questions in AFCAT are mostly direct facts about the human body and diseases. A few also link to flying, such as the effects of altitude on the body.
points: Vitamin deficiencies: A — night blindness, C — scurvy, D — rickets, B1 — beriberi
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium (a protozoan) and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito
Dengue is a viral disease spread by the Aedes mosquito
O negative: universal donor; AB positive: universal recipient
Hypoxia — oxygen shortage at high altitude — is why pilots use oxygen systems

notes.p:
An **ecosystem** includes living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts. Energy flows through food chains: producers → herbivores → carnivores. By the **10% law**, only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next, which is why food chains are short.

**Greenhouse gases** (carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour, CFCs) trap heat and drive global warming. The **ozone layer** in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV rays; it is damaged by **CFCs**.

Key international agreements:
points: Montreal Protocol (1987) — phasing out ozone-depleting substances
Kyoto Protocol (1997) — greenhouse-gas cuts for developed countries
Paris Agreement (2015) — keep warming well below 2°C

notes.p:
India's laws and programmes: **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972**, **Project Tiger (1973)**, **Environment (Protection) Act 1986** (passed after the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy). India has parts of four global **biodiversity hotspots**: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands).

National parks: **Jim Corbett** (Uttarakhand) — India's first national park; **Kaziranga** (Assam) — one-horned rhinoceros; **Gir** (Gujarat) — Asiatic lion; **Sundarbans** (West Bengal) — mangroves and tigers. Numbers of tiger reserves, Ramsar sites and biosphere reserves keep changing — check the latest figures from the Environment Ministry before your exam.

**ISRO** was founded in 1969. **Aryabhata** (1975) was India's first satellite. The **Mars Orbiter Mission** reached Mars orbit in 2014. **Chandrayaan-3** landed near the Moon's south pole on **23 August 2023**, now celebrated as National Space Day. **Aditya-L1** studies the Sun from near the L1 point. India's human spaceflight programme is called **Gaganyaan**, and its astronaut-designates are IAF officers.

Trap: confusing the anemometer (wind speed) with the ammeter (electric current), or the Montreal Protocol (ozone) with the Kyoto Protocol (greenhouse gases).
Pair each item with its keyword and you'll recall it under pressure.
points: Montreal = ozone; Kyoto and Paris = climate

chapters.title: General Awareness: defence, IAF & current affairs

cards.title: Indian Air Force basics
cards.body: The IAF was established on **8 October 1932** (Air Force Day). Motto: 'Nabhah Sprisham Deeptam' — Touch the sky with glory. Arjan Singh is the only officer to hold the five-star rank of Marshal of the Indian Air Force. Air Headquarters is in New Delhi.

cards.title: Aircraft in IAF service (examples)
points: Su-30MKI — Russian-designed, built under licence by HAL
Tejas — indigenous Light Combat Aircraft by HAL
C-17 Globemaster III and C-130J — transport (USA)

cards.title: Air exercises with partners (examples)
points: Tarang Shakti — multinational exercise hosted by India (first held 2024)

cards.title: Current affairs approach
cards.body: For the latest events — appointments, exercises, inductions, sports winners, summits — rely on PIB (pib.gov.in) and one newspaper. Organise notes topic-wise and revise the last 6–8 months before each AFCAT cycle.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Learn the ranks of the IAF in order: Flying Officer, Flight Lieutenant, Squadron Leader, Wing Commander, Group Captain, Air Commodore, Air Vice Marshal, Air Marshal, Air Chief Marshal. Every AFCAT officer is commissioned as a Flying Officer.

cards.q: Air Force Day is celebrated on:
cards.explain: The IAF was established on 8 October 1932.

cards.q: Where is the IAF's Training Command headquartered?
cards.explain: Training Command HQ is in Bengaluru; Maintenance Command is in Nagpur.

cards.q: Who is the only Marshal of the Indian Air Force?
cards.explain: Arjan Singh was conferred the five-star rank of Marshal of the IAF in 2002.

notes.h: The Indian Air Force: core facts
notes.p:
The IAF was established on **8 October 1932**, celebrated as **Air Force Day**. Its motto, **'Nabhah Sprisham Deeptam'** (Touch the sky with glory), comes from the Bhagavad Gita. Air Headquarters is in **New Delhi**. **Air Marshal Subroto Mukerjee** was the first Indian Chief of the Air Staff. **Arjan Singh** is the only officer to hold the five-star rank of **Marshal of the Indian Air Force**.

Rank ladder (every AFCAT officer starts as a **Flying Officer**): Flying Officer → Flight Lieutenant → Squadron Leader → Wing Commander → Group Captain → Air Commodore → Air Vice Marshal → Air Marshal → Air Chief Marshal.
The IAF has **seven commands**:
points: Western — New Delhi; Eastern — Shillong; Central — Prayagraj
Surya Kiran — aerobatic team; Sarang — helicopter display team; Akash Ganga — skydiving team
Garud Commando Force — the IAF's special forces unit

notes.p: Know the origin and role of each major platform:
points: Rafale — French (Dassault) multirole fighter; first jets arrived in 2020 at Ambala
Su-30MKI — Russian-designed, built under licence by HAL; can carry BrahMos
Mirage 2000 — French fighter used in Kargil (1999) and Balakot (2019)
C-17 Globemaster III and C-130J — US transport aircraft
Apache (attack) and Chinook (heavy-lift) — US helicopters; Prachand — indigenous Light Combat Helicopter
Missiles: Astra (air-to-air), Akash (surface-to-air); S-400 — Russian long-range air-defence system

notes.p:
**Flying Officer Nirmal Jit Singh Sekhon** is the only IAF officer awarded the **Param Vir Chakra** (1971, posthumous). **Squadron Leader Rakesh Sharma** became the first Indian in space in 1984 aboard Soyuz T-11. The IAF's role in Kargil was **Operation Safed Sagar** (1999). The **Balakot airstrike** took place on 26 February 2019; **Wing Commander Abhinandan Varthaman** was later awarded the Vir Chakra. The **MiG-21**, the IAF's longest-serving fighter, was retired in September 2025. In 2016, Avani Chaturvedi, Bhawana Kanth and Mohana Singh became the IAF's first women fighter pilots. In 2025, Group Captain **Shubhanshu Shukla** flew to the International Space Station on the Axiom-4 mission.

Joint air exercises: **Garuda** (France), **Cope India** (USA), **Indradhanush** (UK), **Tarang Shakti** (multinational, hosted by India, first held in 2024).

Defence current affairs — appointments, inductions, exercises, operations — change every month. Use **PIB (pib.gov.in)** and the Ministry of Defence's releases as your primary sources and one newspaper for context. Keep topic-wise notes: *Inductions*, *Exercises*, *Appointments*, *Missions*, *Awards*. Revise the last 6–8 months before each AFCAT cycle. For who currently holds a post (Chief of the Air Staff, CDS), always check the latest official source rather than relying on an old book.

Trap: Training Command is in **Bengaluru** and Maintenance Command in **Nagpur** — the swap is a favourite wrong option.
These facts also come up in your AFSB interview.
points: Only MIAF: Arjan Singh; only IAF PVC: Fg Offr N.J.S. Sekhon
Commissioned rank after training: Flying Officer
Garuda — France; Cope India — USA; Indradhanush — UK
First Indian in space: Sqn Ldr Rakesh Sharma (1984)

chapters.title: General Awareness: Indian history — ancient to modern

cards.title: Ancient India
cards.body: The **Indus Valley (Harappan) civilisation** (c. 2600–1900 BCE) had planned cities: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Lothal (dockyard), Dholavira. The **Vedic age** followed. **Buddhism** (Gautama Buddha) and **Jainism** (Mahavira) arose in the 6th century BCE.

cards.title: Empires and rulers
points: Maurya: Chandragupta Maurya; Ashoka (Kalinga war, edicts)
Gupta: Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II — a "classical age"
Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526): Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi
Mughal: Babur (Panipat 1526), Akbar, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb

cards.title: Key battles
points: Panipat I (1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi
Panipat II (1556): Akbar's forces defeated Hemu
Panipat III (1761): Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas
Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764): British rise in Bengal

cards.title: Freedom struggle
cards.body: INC founded **1885**. Partition of Bengal **1905**; Jallianwala Bagh **1919**; Non-Cooperation **1920–22**; Dandi March **1930**; Quit India **1942**; Independence **15 August 1947**.

cards.title: Military history link
cards.body: AFCAT often links history to defence: **Battle of Haldighati** (1576), **Maratha navy** under Kanhoji Angre, **Sikh Khalsa army** under Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and the **INA** of Subhas Chandra Bose.

cards.title: Revise with timelines
cards.body: Make one timeline from 1757 to 1947 with about 30 events. Most history questions in AFCAT are one-liners; a timeline lets you eliminate options by date.

cards.q: Who founded the Maurya Empire?
cards.explain: Chandragupta Maurya founded it, with Chanakya's guidance.

cards.q: The First Battle of Panipat (1526) was won by:
cards.explain: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, founding Mughal rule.

cards.q: The Quit India Movement began in:
cards.explain: Launched in August 1942 ("Do or Die").

notes.p:
The official AFCAT syllabus lists **History** within General Awareness. Questions are factual one-liners: who founded, which battle, which year, which reform. Depth of a degree course is not needed; breadth is.

Split history into four blocks: ancient, medieval, modern (British period) and the national movement. Learn 8–10 anchor facts for each.
points: Ancient: Indus, Vedic, Buddhism/Jainism, Maurya, Gupta

notes.p: The **Harappan** sites show grid planning, drains and the Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro). **Lothal** in Gujarat had a dockyard. The **Mauryas** created the first large pan-Indian empire; **Ashoka** turned to dhamma after the **Kalinga war** and his edicts were written mainly in Prakrit in **Brahmi** script. The **Gupta** period saw advances in mathematics (Aryabhata) and literature (Kalidasa). In the south, the **Cholas** were known for naval expeditions to South-East Asia.

The **Delhi Sultanate** began in 1206 with Qutb-ud-din Aibak. **Alauddin Khalji** introduced market reforms; **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** shifted the capital to Daulatabad and issued token currency. The **Vijayanagara** empire (capital Hampi) peaked under Krishnadeva Raya.

The **Mughals**: Babur won Panipat in 1526; **Akbar** introduced the mansabdari system and Din-i-Ilahi; **Shah Jahan** built the Taj Mahal; **Shivaji** founded the Maratha kingdom and was crowned in 1674.

**Worked recall.** Q. Which Mughal emperor built the Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri?
Step 1: Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital.
Step 2: The gate commemorates his Gujarat campaign.
Answer: **Akbar**. Linking a monument to its builder's capital is a quick way to answer architecture questions.

The East India Company won **Plassey (1757)** and **Buxar (1764)**, gaining Bengal's revenue rights (diwani) in 1765. The **Revolt of 1857** began at Meerut; leaders included Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Tantia Tope, Kunwar Singh and Bahadur Shah Zafar. After it, the **Government of India Act 1858** transferred power to the Crown.

**Worked recall:** Q. Who was Governor-General during the 1857 revolt? Step 1: 1857 → Lord Canning. Step 2: Canning also became the first Viceroy after 1858.

The **INC** was founded in 1885 (A.O. Hume; first president W.C. Bonnerjee). The **Swadeshi movement** followed Bengal's partition in 1905. Gandhi's movements: **Champaran (1917)**, **Non-Cooperation (1920)**, **Civil Disobedience / Dandi March (1930)**, **Quit India (1942)**. Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad and the revolutionaries; Subhas Chandra Bose and the **Indian National Army**. India became independent on **15 August 1947** and a republic on **26 January 1950**.

Important reforms often asked alongside: **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** (Brahmo Samaj, campaign against sati, abolished by Lord William Bentinck in 1829), **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** (widow remarriage, Act of 1856), **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** (Arya Samaj, 1875) and **Jyotiba Phule** (Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873).
History anchors.

chapters.title: General Awareness: geography — India & world

cards.title: Earth basics
cards.body: The Earth's axis is tilted about **23.5°**. The Tropic of Cancer and Capricorn are at 23.5°N and S. Longitudes 15° apart differ by **1 hour** of local time. The **International Date Line** roughly follows 180°.

cards.title: Atmosphere layers
points: Troposphere: weather happens here; temperature falls with height
Stratosphere: ozone layer; jet aircraft often cruise in the lower part

cards.title: India highlights
points: Western Ghats higher than Eastern Ghats
Monsoon June–September; retreating monsoon rains Tamil Nadu

cards.title: Winds and clouds for aviators
cards.body: **Jet streams** are fast upper-air westerly winds; **cumulonimbus** clouds bring thunderstorms and turbulence; **fog** forms when moist air cools near the ground. Pilots must know these well.

cards.title: Map work
cards.body: Learn countries with their capitals, major straits (Malacca, Hormuz, Gibraltar, Palk), and India's neighbours with border lines: Radcliffe (Pakistan, Bangladesh), McMahon (China), Durand (Afghanistan–Pakistan).

cards.q: The ozone layer lies mainly in the:
cards.explain: Most atmospheric ozone is in the stratosphere.

cards.q: The McMahon Line is the boundary between India and:
cards.explain: It is the boundary claimed by India in the eastern sector with China.

cards.q: Places 30° apart in longitude differ in local time by:
cards.explain: 15° = 1 hour, so 30° = 2 hours.

notes.p:
AFCAT General Awareness names **Geography** explicitly. Expect questions on physical geography (Earth, atmosphere, rocks), world records and features, and Indian geography (rivers, soils, climate, resources, national parks).

Because the exam is for an air force, questions about the **atmosphere, weather and clouds** are especially relevant.
points: Know India's river systems and soils

notes.p:
Earth rotates west to east once in about 24 hours, so places to the east see the Sun earlier. **Local time** changes by **4 minutes per degree** of longitude.

**Worked example.** When it is 12:00 noon at Greenwich (0°), what is the local time at 82.5°E?
Step 1: 82.5 × 4 min = 330 min = 5 h 30 min.
Step 2: East is ahead, so time = **5:30 p.m.** — which is why IST = GMT + 5:30.

**Worked example 2.** A flight leaves Delhi (IST) at 10:00 and lands in London 9 hours later when London is on GMT. Local time on landing?
Step 1: Departure in GMT = 10:00 − 5:30 = 04:30 GMT.
Step 2: Add 9 hours = **13:30 local London time**.
(During British Summer Time London is GMT + 1, so check the season.)

The troposphere is thickest at the equator and thinnest at the poles; temperature falls about **6.5°C per km** of height (normal lapse rate). **Jet streams** in the upper troposphere affect flight times. **Cyclones** rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere (Coriolis effect) and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.

Cloud types: **cirrus** (high, wispy), **cumulus** (heaped, fair weather), **stratus** (layer), **nimbus** (rain-bearing), **cumulonimbus** (thunderstorm — dangerous for aircraft).

Learn the major features: the **Nile** is generally listed as the longest river and the **Amazon** carries the most water; the **Pacific** is the largest and deepest ocean (Mariana Trench); **Greenland** is the largest island; **Lake Baikal** is the deepest lake; the **Caspian Sea** is the largest lake by area.

Straits: **Malacca** (Indonesia–Malaysia), **Hormuz** (Iran–Oman, oil route), **Gibraltar** (Spain–Morocco), **Bab-el-Mandeb** (Red Sea–Gulf of Aden), **Palk** (India–Sri Lanka).

India has a **tropical monsoon** climate. Major soils: alluvial (plains), black (Deccan; cotton), red, laterite. Rivers: Ganga (Devprayag), Brahmaputra (Tsangpo in Tibet), Godavari (longest peninsular), Narmada and Tapi (west-flowing). Biosphere reserves and national parks — for example **Jim Corbett** (Uttarakhand, India's first national park), **Kaziranga** (Assam, one-horned rhinoceros), **Gir** (Gujarat, Asiatic lion) — are frequent questions.

India's major ports and resources also appear: **Mumbai** and **Jawaharlal Nehru Port** on the west coast, **Visakhapatnam** (a natural harbour) and **Paradip** on the east. Coal is concentrated in the **Damodar valley** (Jharkhand–West Bengal) and Odisha–Chhattisgarh; petroleum comes from **Mumbai High** offshore, Assam and Gujarat.
Geography one-liners.
points: Ozone in stratosphere; weather in troposphere

chapters.title: General Awareness: civics & Indian polity

cards.title: The Constitution
cards.body: Adopted on **26 November 1949** and in force from **26 January 1950**. Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the **Drafting Committee**; Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Constituent Assembly. The Preamble describes India as a **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic**.

cards.title: Key offices
points: President: elected by an electoral college; Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces
Vice-President: ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha
Prime Minister: head of government; leads Council of Ministers
Lok Sabha: max term 5 years; Rajya Sabha: permanent, one-third retire every 2 years

cards.title: Emergency provisions
cards.body: **Article 352**: national emergency (war, external aggression, armed rebellion). **Article 356**: President's Rule in a state. **Article 360**: financial emergency.

cards.title: Judiciary
cards.body: The **Supreme Court** is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; it issues writs under **Article 32**, high courts under **Article 226**. Writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto.

cards.title: Civics vs politics
cards.body: "Civics" questions ask about citizens' rights and duties, local government (Panchayati Raj — 73rd Amendment; municipalities — 74th), and elections (Election Commission, Art. 324).

cards.q: Who is the Supreme Commander of the Indian Armed Forces?
cards.explain: The supreme command of the Defence Forces is vested in the President.

cards.q: Article 32 provides the right to:
cards.explain: Article 32 lets a citizen move the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights.

cards.q: Panchayati Raj got constitutional status through the:
cards.explain: The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX on panchayats.

notes.p:
The AFCAT syllabus lists **Civics** and **Politics** within General Awareness. That means the Constitution, key institutions, rights and duties, elections and local government — and, occasionally, recent political developments (check current affairs).

The Constitution has a Preamble, many Articles grouped in Parts, and Schedules; the exact numbers have changed through amendments, so learn the important Articles rather than counts.

Fundamental Rights are justiciable — enforceable in court. Article 21 (life and personal liberty) has been interpreted widely by the Supreme Court. **Article 21A** (education for 6–14-year-olds) came through the 86th Amendment. The **right to property** was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment and is now a legal right under Article 300A.

**Directive Principles** (Part IV) are not enforceable in court but guide policy. **Fundamental Duties** (Article 51A) include respecting the flag and anthem and defending the country when called upon.

The **President** is elected indirectly by elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the state Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry). The President can be removed by **impeachment**. The **Prime Minister** is appointed by the President and must command a majority in the **Lok Sabha**.

A **money bill** can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can delay it for at most 14 days. A **joint sitting** (Article 108) is presided over by the Speaker. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House.

The **Vice-President** is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament only, and acts as President when the office is vacant. The **Attorney General** (Article 76) is the government's chief legal adviser and may speak in Parliament without a vote.

The **Supreme Court** hears appeals, gives advisory opinions (Article 143) and protects rights. The **Election Commission** (Article 324) conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. The **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)** created a three-tier panchayat system and urban local bodies, with one-third of seats reserved for women.

**Worked recall:** Q. Which Article deals with President's Rule? Step 1: Emergencies are 352, 356, 360. Step 2: State-level failure → **356**.

Defence is a **Union List** subject. The President is the **Supreme Commander**, but the armed forces work under the Ministry of Defence, headed by the Defence Minister. The **Chief of Defence Staff** post was created in 2019/2020 to head the Department of Military Affairs. Parliament can restrict Fundamental Rights of armed forces members under **Article 33** to ensure discipline.
Polity anchors.
points: Art. 14 equality; Art. 21 life; Art. 32 remedies
Money bill only in Lok Sabha
Art. 33: rights of armed forces may be restricted

chapters.title: Verbal ability: grammar, errors & sentence completion

cards.title: What the section tests
cards.body: Verbal Ability in English covers comprehension, error detection, sentence completion, synonyms, antonyms, vocabulary, and idioms & phrases. The language is simpler than CDS — speed and accuracy matter most.

cards.title: Error detection checklist
cards.body: Check in this order: (1) subject-verb agreement, (2) tense consistency, (3) articles, (4) prepositions, (5) pronoun agreement, (6) adjective/adverb confusion ('He runs quick' → 'quickly'). Most errors fall in the first three.

cards.title: Preposition pairs that are often tested
Sentence completion
cards.body: Read the full sentence and find the clue word. Contrast clues ('but', 'although') signal an opposite meaning; support clues ('and', 'because') signal a similar one. Predict the word before looking at the options.

cards.title: Using a contrast clue
cards.body: 'Although the mission was risky, the pilot remained ___.' 'Although' signals contrast with 'risky', so we need a word meaning calm: **composed**. Options like 'anxious' or 'reckless' fail the contrast.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Do the 25 English questions first if English is your strength — they take less time than numerical ones and set up a calm start for the rest of the paper.

cards.q: Choose the correct word: 'The team consists ___ twelve cadets.'
cards.explain: The correct collocation is 'consists of'.

cards.q: Choose the correct sentence:
cards.explain: 'Drives' is a verb, so it takes the adverb 'carefully'; the subject 'he' needs 'drives'.

cards.q: 'Although he was tired, he ___ the march.' Choose the best word.
cards.explain: 'Although' sets up a contrast with 'tired', so he still completed the march.

notes.p:
AFCAT's verbal ability section includes **error detection, sentence completion, fill in the blanks, synonyms, antonyms, idioms, analogies and a short comprehension**. Grammar questions are moderate in difficulty but time-pressured; aim for about 30 seconds each.

Use a quick checklist on every sentence: subject–verb agreement → tense → pronoun → article → preposition → word choice. Most errors show up within the first two checks.
These eight rules account for most of the errors you will meet. Learn each one with its example sentence.
points: Subject–verb: 'The list of items **is** on the desk' — the subject is 'list'
'Either of', 'neither of', 'each of', 'one of' → singular verb
Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural; joined by 'or/nor' → verb agrees with the nearer one
'Since' with a point of time, 'for' with a period: 'since Monday', 'for three days'
No 'will' after 'if/when' for future conditions: 'When he **arrives**, call me'
Article by sound: an honest man, a European, an X-ray
Avoid double negatives: 'I don't have **any**', not 'I don't have none'

notes.p:
**Example 1.** "Each of the cadets (a) / have been given (b) / a new uniform. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: **(b)** → "has been given". "Each of" is singular.

**Example 2.** "The pilot, as well as his crew, (a) / were awarded (b) / for bravery. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: **(b)** → "was awarded". "As well as" does not make the subject plural.

**Example 3.** "If I will get leave, (a) / I shall visit (b) / my parents. (c) / No error (d)"
Answer: **(a)** → "If I get leave".

notes.h: Sentence completion and fill in the blanks
notes.p:
Read the whole sentence and find the **signal word**. Contrast signals (but, although, despite, however) mean the blank opposes the other part; continuation signals (and, also, moreover, because) mean it agrees.

**Example 4.** "Although the weather was ___, the squadron completed its sortie on time." Options: favourable / clear / hostile / pleasant. "Although" signals contrast with completing on time, so the weather must be bad. Answer: **hostile**.

**Example 5.** "He was so ___ that he never gave up, even after three failures." Options: fickle / persistent / lazy / timid. The second part describes not giving up. Answer: **persistent**.

With +3/−1 marking, a blind guess among four options has zero expected value (¼ × 3 − ¾ × 1 = 0) — it is a pure gamble. But if you can eliminate two options confidently, choosing between the remaining two is a reasonable risk (expected value: ½ × 3 − ½ × 1 = +1).

Common traps: an error placed in the **last part** that hurried readers miss; "No error" sentences that sound formal but are correct; and options in fill-in-the-blanks that fit the meaning but not the grammar (wrong tense or part of speech).
Read this list on the morning of the exam.
points: As well as / along with don't change the subject
Since + point of time; for + period
Find the signal word in sentence completion
Eliminate two options before guessing (+3/−1 marking)
Check the last part — errors hide there too

chapters.title: Verbal ability: vocabulary, idioms & comprehension

cards.title: Synonyms and antonyms
cards.body: These are the fastest marks in the paper. Learn words in groups with their opposites, e.g. brave — valiant, gallant, intrepid; opposite: cowardly, timid. Use the word in a sentence in your head to confirm the fit.

cards.title: Common idioms
points: A piece of cake — very easy
Burn the midnight oil — study or work late into the night
Once in a blue moon — very rarely
Hit the nail on the head — describe exactly what is right
Cry wolf — raise a false alarm

cards.title: Comprehension strategy
cards.body: AFCAT passages are short. Read the questions first, then the passage. Each answer should be traceable to a line in the passage. Title questions: choose the option that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph.

cards.title: Eliminating options
cards.body: Synonym of 'Intrepid': (a) fearful (b) fearless (c) careless (d) tired. 'Intrepid' describes someone who faces danger boldly. (a) is the opposite; (c) and (d) are unrelated. Answer: **fearless**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Make 10 flashcards a day with a word, its meaning and one sentence. In 3 months you will have learnt about 900 words — more than enough for AFCAT.

cards.q: Choose the synonym of 'Intrepid':
cards.explain: Intrepid means fearless and adventurous.

cards.q: 'Once in a blue moon' means:
cards.explain: The idiom means something happens very rarely.

cards.q: Choose the antonym of 'Valiant':
cards.explain: Valiant means brave; its opposite is cowardly.

notes.p: Vocabulary questions — **synonyms, antonyms, idioms, one-word substitutions and verbal analogies** — take seconds when you know the word, so they are worth daily effort. Read an editorial every day, underline new words, and add five to a notebook with meaning, synonym, antonym and your own sentence.

Decide the word's tone (positive/negative), remove options with the wrong tone, then pick the closest meaning. In antonym questions, one option is usually a synonym — cross it out first.

**Example 1.** Synonym of "valiant": (a) cowardly (b) brave (c) weak (d) careless. Answer: **(b) brave**.

**Example 2.** Antonym of "lucid": (a) clear (b) obscure (c) bright (d) simple. Lucid = clear; (a) is a synonym. Answer: **(b) obscure**.

**Example 3.** Antonym of "meticulous": (a) careful (b) thorough (c) careless (d) precise. Answer: **(c) careless**.
An analogy question gives a pair with a relationship and asks you to find a pair with the **same** relationship. First state the relationship in a sentence, then test each option with that sentence.
points: Pilot : Aircraft :: Captain : Ship (person who commands)
Example: 'Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?' — sentence: 'works in'. Answer: School

notes.p: Learn idioms as whole phrases with an example situation; one-word substitutions are easier to remember when grouped by theme — here, a few with an Air Force flavour.
points: To fly off the handle — to lose one's temper suddenly
A blessing in disguise — something good that first seemed bad
To keep one's fingers crossed — to hope for success
Cool as a cucumber — very calm
Aviary — place where birds are kept; Hangar — shelter for aircraft
Veteran — person with long experience; Novice — beginner
Mutiny — rebellion by soldiers or sailors against officers

notes.p: AFCAT passages are usually short. Read the questions first, then the passage. Answer only from the passage, prefer moderate options over extreme ones ("always", "never"), and for title questions choose the option that covers the whole passage. Don't spend more than 4–5 minutes on one passage; if a question is unclear, move on and return.
Five minutes with this list before the exam.
points: Check tone first in synonym/antonym questions
Antonym options usually hide a synonym
Analogies: state the relationship as a sentence
Up in the air = undecided; fly off the handle = lose temper
RC: answer only from the passage
Five new words a day, revised weekly

chapters.title: Verbal ability: reading comprehension & cloze

cards.title: Passage questions
cards.body: A short passage (usually 150–350 words) is followed by questions on the **main idea**, **specific details**, **inference**, **vocabulary in context** and **tone**. Answers must come from the passage, not from outside knowledge.

cards.title: Read questions first?
cards.body: Skim the questions first so you know what to look for, then read the passage once carefully. Detail questions can be answered by locating keywords; main-idea questions need the whole passage.

cards.title: Question types
points: Main idea: what the whole passage is mostly about
Detail: stated directly — find the line
Inference: not stated, but must be true
Vocabulary: meaning as used in that sentence

cards.title: Cloze test
cards.body: A paragraph with blanks. Read the full paragraph first, then fill blanks using grammar (part of speech, tense) and meaning (logic, tone). Re-read with all blanks filled.

cards.title: Inference vs extreme
cards.body: Passage: "Many pilots report fatigue on long night flights." An option saying "**All** pilots are fatigued" is too extreme; "Night flights can cause pilot fatigue" is a valid inference.

cards.title: Eliminate
cards.body: Reject options that are **out of scope**, **too extreme** (always, never, all), **opposite** to the passage, or true in real life but **not stated**.

cards.q: In RC, an option that is factually true in real life but not supported by the passage should be:
options: chosen if it has keywords from the passage
cards.explain: Answers must be supported by the passage itself.

cards.q: Which word usually signals an option is too extreme?
cards.explain: "Always" makes a sweeping claim that a passage rarely supports.

cards.q: In a cloze test, the first thing to do is:
cards.explain: Reading the whole paragraph first gives the theme and tone.

notes.p:
**Comprehension** is the first item in the official AFCAT Verbal Ability syllabus, followed by error detection, sentence completion, synonyms, antonyms, vocabulary, and idioms and phrases. Passages are short and questions direct, but they take time, so a method saves minutes for the reasoning section.

Passages often come from general topics: environment, technology, history, human behaviour or defence.
points: Read actively — ask "what is the author's point?"
Mark keywords and turning points (but, however)

notes.p:
**Step 1:** Glance at the questions (10 seconds).
**Step 2:** Read the passage once; note the main idea of each paragraph in two or three words.
**Step 3:** For detail questions, locate the line and match the meaning, not just the words.
**Step 4:** For inference questions, choose the option that **must** be true based on the passage.
**Step 5:** For vocabulary questions, substitute each option into the sentence.

This takes about 4–5 minutes for a passage with 4–5 questions.

Passage (summary): "Radar was developed rapidly during the Second World War. It allowed defenders to detect incoming aircraft long before they were visible, giving fighter squadrons time to take off. However, early radar could not easily tell friendly aircraft from enemy ones, which led to the development of identification systems."

**Q1. Main idea?** Step 1: The passage describes radar's wartime role and a limitation. Answer: radar's development and early use in air defence.
**Q2. Which is an inference?** (a) Radar made fighters unnecessary — contradicts the passage. (b) Early radar could cause confusion between friend and foe — supported by "could not easily tell". Answer: **(b)**.
**Q3. "Rapidly" is closest to:** quickly.

A cloze passage tests vocabulary and grammar together. For each blank, decide: (1) part of speech, (2) singular/plural or tense, (3) meaning suggested by neighbouring sentences.

**Example.** "The pilot remained ___ despite the engine failure, and landed the aircraft safely." Options: anxious, calm, careless, sleepy. The contrast "despite" and the result "landed safely" → **calm**.

**Example 2.** "Regular practice ___ confidence; without it, even a talented cadet may ___ under pressure." Options for blank 1: destroys, builds, hides, delays. Options for blank 2: excel, falter, relax, succeed. The semicolon sets up a contrast ("without it"), so blank 1 is positive (**builds**) and blank 2 negative (**falter**).

Choosing an option because it repeats words from the passage (a common decoy); choosing an attractive "real-world" fact; ignoring words like "not" or "except" in the question; and over-reading — spending more than about five minutes on one passage.

Tone questions ask about the author's attitude. Common answers are **objective/neutral** (just reports facts), **critical** (points out faults), **appreciative** (praises), **cautionary** (warns) and **ironic** (says the opposite of what is meant). Look at adjectives and adverbs the author chooses — words like "unfortunately" or "remarkably" reveal attitude.
Comprehension checklist.
points: Inference: must be true from text

chapters.title: Verbal ability: idioms & phrases

cards.title: What an idiom is
cards.body: An **idiom** is a fixed expression whose meaning differs from its literal words. "Break the ice" means to start a conversation in an awkward situation, not to crack ice.

cards.title: Common idioms (A–H)
points: A bolt from the blue: a sudden surprise
At the eleventh hour: at the last moment
Bite the bullet: face a painful situation bravely
Burn the midnight oil: work late into the night
Cry over spilt milk: regret what cannot be undone
Hit the nail on the head: say exactly the right thing

cards.title: Common idioms (I–Z)
points: Once in a blue moon: very rarely
A wild goose chase: a useless search
Take the bull by the horns: face a problem directly

cards.title: In context
cards.body: "The match was **called off** due to rain." Called off = **cancelled**, not "announced".

cards.title: Method
cards.body: If you do not know an idiom, picture the literal image and ask what it might suggest; then check which option fits the sentence. Avoid options that just repeat the literal words.

cards.q: "At the eleventh hour" means:
cards.explain: It means just before it is too late.

cards.q: "To turn a deaf ear" means:
cards.explain: It means deliberately ignoring a request or advice.

cards.q: "Put off" in "The meeting was put off till Monday" means:
cards.explain: Put off = postpone.

notes.p:
**Idioms and phrases** are named in the AFCAT verbal syllabus. A typical question gives a sentence with an idiom underlined and four meanings; sometimes it asks you to fill a blank with the right idiom or phrasal verb.

Idioms cannot be worked out by grammar; they must be learnt. But many have logical origins that help memory: "bite the bullet" comes from soldiers biting a bullet during surgery without anaesthetic.
points: Learn 10 idioms a day with one sentence each
Revise idioms by theme: success, failure, anger, time
Phrasal verbs change meaning with the particle

notes.p:
**Effort and work:** burn the midnight oil, put one's shoulder to the wheel (work hard), go the extra mile.
**Trouble:** in hot water, in a fix, between the devil and the deep sea (between two equally bad choices), a hornet's nest (a troublesome situation).
**Time:** once in a blue moon, at the eleventh hour, in the nick of time (just in time), call it a day (stop working).
**Behaviour:** turn over a new leaf (change for the better), show the white feather (show cowardice), bury the hatchet (make peace), pay lip service (support in words only).
**Success/failure:** a feather in one's cap (an achievement), fall flat (fail), go to the dogs (be ruined).

A phrasal verb is a verb + particle with a new meaning. The same verb changes sense with different particles:
• **Bring up**: raise a child or mention a topic; **bring about**: cause.
• **Look after**: take care of; **look into**: investigate; **look down upon**: despise.
• **Give up**: abandon; **give in**: surrender; **give away**: distribute or reveal.
• **Break down**: stop working; **break out**: start suddenly (war, fire); **break into**: enter by force.

**Example 1.** "After failing twice, he decided to **turn over a new leaf**."
Step 1: Context — failure, then a decision.
Step 2: Options: start reading, change his behaviour for the better, give up, travel.
Answer: **change his behaviour for the better**.

**Example 2.** "The news of his selection came as **a bolt from the blue**." Answer: **a complete surprise**.

**Example 3.** Fill in: "Fire ___ in the hangar late at night." Options: broke out, broke in, broke down, broke up. Answer: **broke out**.

Choosing the literal meaning; confusing similar idioms (a "red-letter day" is a memorable day, while "to see red" is to become angry); and ignoring tense or particle in phrasal-verb blanks. When two meanings look close, test both in the sentence. Also beware of mixing up "to get cold feet" (to become nervous and back out) with "to give the cold shoulder" (to ignore someone deliberately).
Idiom list to revise.
points: Bolt from the blue: sudden surprise
Bite the bullet: face pain bravely
Call off: cancel; put off: postpone

chapters.title: Numerical ability: decimals, ratio & average

cards.title: Ratio and proportion
points: Divide N in ratio a:b → aN/(a + b) and bN/(a + b)
If a:b = c:d, then ad = bc
Combine a:b and b:c by making b equal in both

cards.title: Average
points: Average of first n natural numbers = (n + 1)/2
If every value rises by k, the average rises by k

cards.title: Dividing in a ratio
cards.body: Divide ₹1,200 between A and B in the ratio 3:5. Total parts = 8; one part = 1,200/8 = 150. A gets 3 × 150 = **₹450**, B gets 5 × 150 = **₹750**.

cards.title: Removing a number from an average
cards.body: The average of 5 numbers is 20, so their sum is 100. After removing one number, the average of the other 4 is 18, so their sum is 72. The removed number = 100 − 72 = **28**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: AFCAT's numerical section has fewer questions than the other sections but they take longer. Memorise the fraction-percent table — it turns many calculations into mental maths.

cards.q: The average of the first 10 natural numbers is:
If a:b = 2:3 and b:c = 4:5, then a:c is:
cards.explain: a:b:c = 8:12:15 (multiply to make b = 12), so a:c = 8:15.

cards.q: 0.125 expressed as a fraction is:

notes.p: Convert between fractions and decimals instantly — it saves a lot of time:
points: BODMAS order: Brackets, Orders (powers/roots), Division/Multiplication (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right)

notes.p:
A ratio a : b compares two quantities of the same kind. To **divide an amount** in a ratio, divide by the sum of the parts.

**Example 1.** Divide ₹1,200 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5.
Step 1: Total parts = 10, so one part = ₹120.
Step 2: Shares = ₹240, ₹360, ₹600. (Check: 240 + 360 + 600 = 1,200 ✓.)

**Example 2.** If a : b = 2 : 3 and b : c = 4 : 5, find a : b : c.
Step 1: Make b equal: multiply the first by 4 and the second by 3 → a : b = 8 : 12, b : c = 12 : 15.
Step 2: a : b : c = **8 : 12 : 15**.

Proportion terms: **mean proportional** of a and b = √(ab) (of 4 and 9 it is 6); **third proportional** to a and b = b²/a (to 4 and 6 it is 36/4 = 9); **fourth proportional** to a, b, c = bc/a.

Average = sum of observations / number of observations. Two powerful shortcuts: the average of consecutive numbers is the **middle value**, and if every value changes by k, the average changes by k.

**Example 3.** A batsman's average after 10 innings is 30. He scores 74 in the 11th. New average?
Step 1: Old total = 300. New total = 374.
Step 2: New average = 374/11 = **34**.

**Example 4.** The average of 10 numbers was found to be 25, but 64 was wrongly read as 46. Correct average?
Step 1: Wrong total = 250. Error = 64 − 46 = 18.
Step 2: Correct average = 268/10 = **26.8**.

**Alligation** gives the ratio in which two items at different prices must be mixed to get a mean price: (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper).

**Example 5.** Rice at ₹40/kg and ₹55/kg is mixed to sell at ₹45/kg (cost price of mixture). Ratio?
Step 1: Cheaper : dearer = (55 − 45) : (45 − 40) = 10 : 5 = **2 : 1**.

**Example 6.** The ages of A and B are in the ratio 3 : 4. After 5 years the ratio will be 4 : 5. Find their ages.
Step 1: Let the ages be 3x and 4x. Then (3x + 5)/(4x + 5) = 4/5.
Step 2: 15x + 25 = 16x + 20 ⇒ x = 5.
Step 3: Ages = **15 and 20**. Check: 20/25 = 4/5 ✓.

Trap: in alligation, the order is reversed — the cheaper item's share comes from (dearer − mean).
Learn the fraction–decimal table until it is automatic.
points: Divide by the sum of ratio parts
Equalise the common term to combine ratios
Corrected average: adjust the total, then divide
Age problems: let ages be multiples of x

chapters.title: Numerical ability: percentage, profit & interest

cards.title: Percentage shortcuts
points: x% of y = y% of x
If A is r% more than B, B is r/(100 + r) × 100 % less than A
Successive change a% then b%: net = a + b + ab/100
Price up by r% → cut consumption by r/(100 + r) × 100 % to keep spending the same

cards.title: Profit, loss and discount
points: Discount is always on the marked price (MP)

cards.title: Simple interest
points: Money doubles under SI in 100/R years

cards.title: Discount and profit together
cards.body: An article's marked price is ₹1,000 and a 10% discount is given, so SP = ₹900. If the cost price is ₹750, profit = 150 and profit % = 150/750 × 100 = **20%**.

cards.title: More than / less than
cards.body: A's salary is 20% more than B's. By what percent is B's salary less than A's? 20/120 × 100 = **16⅔%**. Using B = 100, A = 120 makes this clear.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Assume 100 as the starting value in every percentage question. It removes algebra and avoids sign mistakes.

cards.q: Simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years is:
A price rises by 10% and then falls by 10%. The net change is:
A shopkeeper buys an item for ₹200 and sells it for ₹180. The loss percentage is:

notes.p:
Fast percentage work depends on knowing fraction equivalents: 50% = 1/2, 25% = 1/4, 20% = 1/5, 12.5% = 1/8, 33⅓% = 1/3, 16⅔% = 1/6, 11.11% = 1/9, 10% = 1/10.

**Successive change formula:** two changes of a% and b% give a net change of **a + b + ab/100** (use negative values for decreases).

Profit % = (profit/CP) × 100; loss % = (loss/CP) × 100. **Marked price (MP)** is the listed price; **discount** is calculated on MP. SP = MP − discount.

**Example 1.** An article costing ₹800 is sold at a 15% loss. SP = 800 × 0.85 = **₹680**.

**Example 2.** MP = ₹1,000, discount 20%, CP = ₹640. Profit %?
Step 1: SP = 1,000 × 0.8 = ₹800.
Step 2: Profit = 800 − 640 = ₹160.
Step 3: Profit % = 160/640 × 100 = **25%**.

**Example 3.** A shopkeeper uses a 900 g weight instead of 1 kg and sells at cost price. Gain %?
Step 1: He gives 900 g but charges for 1,000 g, gaining 100 g.
Step 2: Gain % = 100/900 × 100 = **11.11%**.

**Special case:** two items sold at the **same SP**, one at x% profit and one at x% loss, always give an overall **loss of x²/100 %**. For x = 20, loss = 4%.

SI = (P × R × T)/100. Amount = P + SI.

**Example 4.** P = ₹5,000, R = 8% p.a., T = 3 years. SI = 5,000 × 8 × 3/100 = **₹1,200**.

**Example 5.** A sum doubles in 8 years at simple interest. Rate?
Step 1: SI = P in 8 years ⇒ P = P × R × 8/100.
Step 2: R = 100/8 = **12.5%**.

Amount = P(1 + R/100)ᵀ; CI = Amount − P. For half-yearly compounding, halve the rate and double the number of periods.

**Example 6.** P = ₹8,000, R = 5% p.a., 2 years, compounded annually.
Step 1: Amount = 8,000 × 1.05 × 1.05 = 8,000 × 1.1025 = ₹8,820.
Step 2: CI = **₹820**.
Step 3: SI for the same = 8,000 × 5 × 2/100 = ₹800, so CI − SI = ₹20 = 8,000 × (5/100)². ✓

Traps: calculating profit % on SP; applying a discount to CP instead of MP; and forgetting to halve the rate for half-yearly compounding.
These shortcuts can save 20–30 seconds per question.
points: Profit/loss % on CP; discount on MP

chapters.title: Numerical ability: time, speed, distance & work

cards.title: Speed basics
points: Average speed for equal distances at x and y = 2xy/(x + y)

cards.title: Trains
points: Crossing a pole or person: time = train length / speed
Crossing a platform: time = (train + platform length) / speed
Opposite directions: relative speed = sum; same direction = difference

cards.title: Boats and streams
points: Boat speed in still water = (D + U)/2

cards.title: Time and work
points: If A can do a job in a days, A's 1-day work = 1/a
A and B together: ab/(a + b) days
Pipes: filling pipe adds, leak/emptying pipe subtracts

cards.title: Train past a pole
cards.body: A 150 m train runs at 54 km/h. Speed = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s. Time to pass a pole = 150/15 = **10 seconds**.

cards.title: Work together
cards.body: A can finish a task in 12 days and B in 24 days. Together: (12 × 24)/(12 + 24) = 288/36 = **8 days**.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Convert all units first (km/h to m/s, hours to minutes). Most wrong answers in this topic come from mixed units, not from wrong methods.

cards.q: A boat goes 12 km/h downstream and 8 km/h upstream. The speed of the stream is:
A man covers equal distances at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. His average speed is:
A 200 m train at 72 km/h crosses a 100 m platform in:
cards.explain: Speed = 20 m/s; distance = 200 + 100 = 300 m; time = 300/20 = 15 s.

notes.p:
Distance = speed × time. To convert **km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18**; m/s to km/h, multiply by 18/5. So 72 km/h = 20 m/s and 54 km/h = 15 m/s.

**Average speed** = total distance / total time — **not** the average of speeds. For equal distances at x and y, average speed = **2xy/(x + y)**.

**Example 1.** A car goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns at 60 km/h. Average speed?
Step 1: 2 × 40 × 60/(40 + 60) = 4,800/100 = **48 km/h** (not 50).

A train passing a pole or a person covers its **own length**; passing a platform or bridge, it covers **its length + the platform's length**. Relative speed: same direction → subtract; opposite directions → add.

**Example 2.** A 200 m train at 72 km/h crosses a 300 m platform. Time?
Step 1: Speed = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.
Step 2: Distance = 200 + 300 = 500 m.
Step 3: Time = 500/20 = **25 s**.

**Example 3.** Trains of 120 m and 80 m run in opposite directions at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. Time to cross each other?
Step 1: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
Step 2: Distance = 120 + 80 = 200 m.
Step 3: Time = 200/25 = **8 s**.

If the boat's speed in still water is u and the stream's speed is v: **downstream = u + v**, **upstream = u − v**. So u = (down + up)/2 and v = (down − up)/2.

**Example 4.** Downstream speed 15 km/h, upstream 9 km/h. Then boat = (15 + 9)/2 = **12 km/h**, stream = (15 − 9)/2 = **3 km/h**.

The same logic applies to aircraft with **tailwind** (adds to speed) and **headwind** (reduces speed) — a nice link for an Air Force exam.

notes.h: Time and work, pipes and cisterns
notes.p:
Use the **LCM (efficiency) method**: take total work as the LCM of the days, then find units per day.

**Example 5.** A does a job in 10 days, B in 15 days. Together?
Step 1: Total work = LCM(10, 15) = 30 units.
Step 2: A does 3 units/day, B does 2 units/day, together 5.
Step 3: Time = 30/5 = **6 days**.

**Example 6.** A pipe fills a tank in 6 hours; an outlet empties it in 9 hours. Both open?
Step 1: Net rate = 1/6 − 1/9 = 3/18 − 2/18 = 1/18.
Step 2: Tank fills in **18 hours**.

**Man-days rule:** M₁D₁H₁ = M₂D₂H₂ (for the same work). If 12 men finish in 15 days, 18 men need 12 × 15/18 = **10 days**.

Traps: averaging speeds directly, forgetting to add the platform length, and adding an outlet pipe's rate instead of subtracting it.
Write the key formulas on your rough sheet first.
points: Opposite directions add speeds; same direction subtract
Work: use LCM units per day
Outlet pipe = negative rate; M₁D₁ = M₂D₂

chapters.title: Numerical ability: decimal fractions & simplification

cards.title: Decimal fractions
cards.body: A **decimal fraction** has a power of 10 as denominator: 0.7 = 7/10, 0.07 = 7/100. To convert a decimal to a fraction, write it over the right power of 10 and simplify.

cards.title: Operations
points: Multiply: count total decimal places in both factors
Divide: shift decimal in both until divisor is whole

cards.title: BODMAS and approximation
cards.body: Simplify in order: Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. For approximation questions, round numbers sensibly (e.g. 49.97 ≈ 50), compute, then pick the closest option.

cards.title: Speed
cards.body: Turn awkward decimals into fractions: 0.125 × 64 = 64/8 = **8**; 0.375 × 48 = 3/8 × 48 = **18**.

cards.q: 0.04 × 0.5 equals:
cards.explain: 4 × 5 = 20 with 3 decimal places → 0.020.

cards.q: 2.5 ÷ 0.05 equals:
cards.explain: Multiply both by 100: 250 ÷ 5 = 50.

cards.q: Which is the largest?
cards.explain: Compare digit by digit: 0.7000 > 0.6999.

notes.p:
The first topic in the official AFCAT numerical syllabus is **decimal fraction**. Each place to the right of the decimal point is a tenth of the one before: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Adding zeros at the end of a decimal does not change its value (0.5 = 0.50), but a zero right after the point does (0.05 ≠ 0.5).

To compare decimals, make them the same length by adding zeros, then compare as whole numbers: 0.7 vs 0.69 → 70 vs 69.
points: Terminating decimals have only 2s and 5s in the denominator
Multiplying by 10 shifts the point right

notes.p:
**Example 1.** Simplify 3.6 × 0.25 ÷ 0.009.
Step 1: 3.6 × 0.25 = 0.9 (36 × 25 = 900, three decimal places → 0.900).
Step 2: 0.9 ÷ 0.009 = 900 ÷ 9 = **100**.

**Example 2.** Simplify (0.6 × 0.6 + 0.4 × 0.4 + 2 × 0.6 × 0.4).
Step 1: This is a² + b² + 2ab = (a + b)².
Step 2: (0.6 + 0.4)² = 1² = **1**.

Recognising algebraic identities is the fastest way through "simplify" questions.

To order fractions, either convert to decimals or cross-multiply. **Example 3.** Arrange 3/5, 5/8, 7/11 in ascending order.
Step 1: Decimals: 0.6, 0.625, 0.636…
Step 2: Ascending: **3/5 < 5/8 < 7/11**.

Shortcut: when numerator and denominator both increase by the same amount and the fraction is below 1, the fraction gets larger (3/5 → 5/7 → 7/9).

**Example 5.** Convert 0.36̄ (only 6 recurring) to a fraction.
Step 1: Number formed by all digits minus non-recurring part: 36 − 3 = 33.
Step 2: Denominator: one 9 (recurring digit) and one 0 (non-recurring digit) → 90.
Step 3: 33/90 = **11/30**.

AFCAT often gives "approximately equal to" questions.

**Example 4.** 39.97% of 600.12 + 14.98 × 6.02 ≈ ?
Step 1: Round: 40% of 600 = 240; 15 × 6 = 90.
Step 2: 240 + 90 = **330** (pick the nearest option).

Apply BODMAS strictly: 12 + 6 ÷ 3 × 2 = 12 + 2 × 2 = 16, not 12.

Miscounting decimal places in multiplication; dividing by a decimal without shifting the point in both numbers; and treating 0.1 × 0.1 as 0.1. In approximation, rounding every number in the same direction can push you to the wrong option — round some up and some down.

Time matters: numerical ability has relatively few questions in AFCAT, but each simplification question should take under a minute. If a calculation is getting long, look again for an identity, a fraction shortcut or an approximation — the setters usually intend one.
Decimal essentials.
points: Count total decimal places to multiply
Approximate to the nearest round number

chapters.title: Numerical ability: averages, ratio & proportion — deeper practice

cards.title: Average formulas
points: Average of first n natural numbers = (n + 1)/2
New average after adding x: (nA + x)/(n + 1)

cards.title: Replacement problems
cards.body: If one value is replaced and the average of n items changes by d, then **new value − old value = n × d**.

cards.title: Ratio tools
points: Divide N in a : b → aN/(a + b) and bN/(a + b)
Compound ratio of a:b and c:d = ac : bd
Mean proportional of a and b = √(ab)

cards.title: Weighted average
cards.body: Section A: 30 students average 60. Section B: 20 students average 70. Combined = (1,800 + 1,400)/50 = **64**.

cards.title: Ratio of coins
cards.body: A bag has ₹1, 50 p and 25 p coins in ratio 1 : 2 : 4, worth ₹60 in all. Value ratio = 1 : 1 : 1 → each worth ₹20 → **20, 40, 80** coins.

cards.title: Ages
cards.body: Ratio of ages problems: write present ages as ak and bk, then shift both by the same years. The age **difference** never changes.

cards.q: The average of 5 numbers is 20. If one number, 30, is removed, the new average is:
₹1,200 is divided between A and B in the ratio 5 : 3. B gets:
The average age of a team of 11 is 25. When the coach is included it becomes 26. Coach's age:

notes.p:
**Average** and **ratio & proportion** are separate items in the official AFCAT numerical syllabus. An average is a balancing point: values above it exactly balance values below it. So instead of adding everything, add only **deviations** from a guessed average.

**Example 1.** Average of 47, 52, 49, 55, 47.
Step 1: Assume 50; deviations −3, +2, −1, +5, −3 = 0.
Step 2: Average = 50 + 0/5 = **50**.
points: Adding a constant to all values adds it to the average
Multiplying all values by k multiplies the average by k

notes.p:
**Example 2.** The average weight of 8 men rises by 1.5 kg when one man weighing 65 kg is replaced by a new man. Weight of the new man?
Step 1: Total increase = 8 × 1.5 = 12 kg.
Step 2: New man = 65 + 12 = **77 kg**.

**Example 3.** A batsman scores 87 in his 17th innings and raises his average by 3. New average?
Step 1: Let the old average be x: 16x + 87 = 17(x + 3).
Step 2: 16x + 87 = 17x + 51 → x = 36.
Step 3: New average = **39**.

Ratios compare; proportions equate two ratios. Combine ratios through a common term: A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5 → make B = 12: A : B : C = **8 : 12 : 15**.

**Example 4.** Two numbers are in ratio 3 : 5. If 9 is subtracted from each, the ratio becomes 12 : 23. Find the numbers.
Step 1: (3k − 9)/(5k − 9) = 12/23.
Step 2: 69k − 207 = 60k − 108 → 9k = 99 → k = 11.
Step 3: Numbers **33 and 55**.

**Example 5.** The ratio of A's and B's ages is 4 : 3. After 6 years it will be 11 : 9. Present age of A?
Step 1: (4k + 6)/(3k + 6) = 11/9.
Step 2: 36k + 54 = 33k + 66 → 3k = 12 → k = 4.
Step 3: A = **16 years** (B = 12).

Partnership: profit is shared in the ratio of **capital × time**.

Averaging averages of groups of different sizes (use weights); forgetting to include the new member in the count; and treating ratio numbers as actual quantities. In "average speed" questions, never average speeds directly — use total distance over total time.
Averages and ratios.
points: Write ratio terms as ak, bk
Combine ratios via the common term

chapters.title: Reasoning: verbal reasoning

cards.title: What to expect
cards.body: The Reasoning & Military Aptitude section has the most questions in AFCAT. Verbal reasoning covers analogies, odd one out, number and letter series, coding-decoding, blood relations and directions. These reward practice more than any other section.

cards.title: Coding-decoding
cards.body: If CAT is coded as DBU, each letter moves +1 (C→D, A→B, T→U). So DOG becomes **EPH**. Always test the rule on every letter before applying it.

cards.title: Directions
cards.body: A cadet walks 3 km north, then turns right and walks 4 km. Turning right from north means facing east. Distance from start = √(3² + 4²) = **5 km**, in the north-east direction.

cards.title: Blood relations
cards.body: Draw a family tree with symbols: + for male, − for female, horizontal lines for couples, vertical lines for generations. Example: 'He is the only son of my father' (said by a woman) means he is her brother.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Write the alphabet with position numbers (A1…Z26) on your rough sheet at the start. It speeds up every letter-series and coding question.

cards.q: Find the next number: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ?
cards.explain: Differences are 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next difference is 12: 30 + 12 = 42 (also n(n + 1) for n = 6).

cards.q: If CAT is coded as DBU, how is DOG coded?
cards.explain: Each letter shifts one place forward: D→E, O→P, G→H.

cards.q: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?
cards.explain: A doctor works in a hospital; a teacher works in a school.

notes.p: The reasoning section of AFCAT (along with military aptitude) includes **number and letter series, coding–decoding, analogies, odd one out, blood relations, directions, ranking and simple syllogisms**. These questions are not hard individually; the challenge is speed. A clear method for each type turns them into quick marks.

For **number series**, check differences first, then ratios, then squares/cubes, then alternate terms.

**Example 1.** 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, ? — differences 4, 6, 8, 10 → next difference 12 → **42**. (These are n(n + 1).)

For **letters**, learn positions: A1 … Z26. The word **EJOTY** gives 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 — handy anchors. Opposite letters add to 27 (A–Z, B–Y, M–N).

**Example 2.** If CAT is coded as DBU, how is DOG coded?
Step 1: C→D, A→B, T→U — each letter moves +1.
Step 2: D→E, O→P, G→H. Answer: **EPH**.

Always draw. Right turn from north is east; left turn from north is west.

**Example 3.** Ravi walks 5 km north, turns right and walks 3 km, then turns right and walks 9 km. How far and in which direction is he from the start?
Step 1: North 5 → (0, 5). Right = east 3 → (3, 5). Right again = south 9 → (3, −4).
Step 2: Distance = √(3² + 4²) = **5 km**, towards the **south-east**.

**Example 4.** Pointing to a man, Riya says, "He is the son of my grandfather's only son." Who is he?
Step 1: Grandfather's only son = Riya's father.
Step 2: Father's son = **Riya's brother**.

notes.h: Ranking, odd one out and syllogisms
notes.p:
**Ranking:** total = (rank from top) + (rank from bottom) − 1. If Ravi is 7th from the top and 12th from the bottom, there are 7 + 12 − 1 = **18** students.

**Odd one out:** look for category (all fruits but one vegetable), property (all primes but one), or pattern (letters with a fixed gap). Example: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 — **9** is the only non-prime.

**Syllogisms:** draw Venn diagrams. "All A are B" and "Some B are C" do **not** guarantee "Some A are C" — the C circle may overlap B outside A. Only accept a conclusion if it is true in **every** possible diagram.

Attempt the types you are fastest at first. Don't spend more than 45–60 seconds on any reasoning question; mark it and move on. Common traps: forgetting that the person turns relative to the direction they **currently face**; assuming gender in blood-relation questions when it isn't given; and accepting "possible" conclusions in syllogisms as definite.
Practise 30 mixed questions daily to build rhythm.
points: Series: differences → ratios → squares → alternate terms
Always draw direction and family-tree diagrams
Total in a row = top rank + bottom rank − 1
Syllogism conclusion must hold in every diagram
Skip after a minute; come back later

chapters.title: Reasoning: mirror, water images & figure series

cards.title: Mirror images
cards.body: A vertical mirror (placed to the right or left) swaps left and right but keeps top and bottom. Letters symmetric about a vertical axis — A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y — look the same in such a mirror.

cards.title: Water images
cards.body: A water image is a reflection about a horizontal line: top and bottom swap, left and right stay. Letters symmetric about a horizontal axis — B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X — look the same.

cards.title: Clock in a mirror
points: Mirror time = 11:60 − actual time (for times between 1:00 and 11:00)
For times after 11:00, use 23:60 − actual time

cards.title: Figure series and embedded figures
cards.body: In figure series, track one element at a time: rotation (45°/90° clockwise or anticlockwise), number of lines, shading and position. In embedded figures, the given shape must appear exactly — same size and orientation — inside one of the options.

cards.title: Rotation rule
cards.body: An arrow points up, then right, then down. Each step rotates it 90° clockwise. The next figure will point **left**. Always check whether the rotation is clockwise or anticlockwise before choosing.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Spatial questions look hard but become routine with practice. Solve 20 mixed figure questions every day for a month — speed improves dramatically.

cards.q: A clock shows 3:15. What time appears in a mirror?
Which letter looks the same in a vertical mirror?
cards.explain: A is symmetric about a vertical axis, so its mirror image is unchanged.

cards.q: Which letter looks the same in its water image?
cards.explain: B is symmetric about a horizontal axis, so its water image is unchanged.

notes.p:
A **mirror image** (vertical mirror placed to the right or left) swaps **left and right** but keeps top and bottom unchanged. Capital letters symmetric about a vertical axis look the same in such a mirror: **A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y**.

For a word, two things happen: the **order of letters reverses** and **each letter is flipped**. So the mirror image of "AFCAT" shows T first (unchanged, since T is symmetric) and the F and C reversed. When options look similar, check an asymmetric letter like F, C, R or N — that is where the wrong options differ.

A **water image** is a reflection about a horizontal line: **top and bottom swap**, left and right stay. Letters symmetric about a horizontal axis look the same: **B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O, X**. Numbers: 0, 3 and 8 keep their shape in a water image.

Letters symmetric about **both** axes — **H, I, O, X** — are unchanged in both mirror and water images. This makes them useful checkpoints.

A clock seen in a mirror shows a time that, added to the real time, makes 12:00.

**Rule:** for times between 1:00 and 11:00, mirror time = **11:60 − actual time**; for times between 11:00 and 1:00, use **23:60 − actual time**.

**Example 1.** Actual time 4:20. Mirror time = 11:60 − 4:20 = **7:40**.
**Example 2.** Actual time 10:50. Mirror time = 11:60 − 10:50 = **1:10**.
**Example 3.** Actual time 12:20. Mirror time = 23:60 − 12:20 = 11:40.
Check Example 1: 4:20 + 7:40 = 12:00 ✓.
Track **one element at a time**:
points: Rotation: 45° or 90° steps, clockwise or anticlockwise
Count: lines, dots or sides increasing by a fixed number
Shading: moves position or alternates filled/empty
Position: an element moves around corners in a fixed direction
Example: an arrow points up, right, down — rotating 90° clockwise — so next it points left
Figure analogy: find the change from figure 1 to 2, then apply the same change to figure 3

notes.p:
In **embedded figures**, the given shape must appear in an option with the **same size and orientation** — it cannot be rotated or scaled. Trace its most distinctive corner or angle first and look for that in each option.

In **pattern completion**, a square pattern has a missing piece. Most patterns are symmetric left–right, top–bottom or both. Check the lines that should continue across the missing piece's edges; eliminate options where lines don't meet.

Trap: in mirror questions, students often flip top and bottom as well — that would be a water image. Ask yourself first: "Is the mirror vertical or horizontal?"
Twenty mixed figure questions a day for a month builds real speed.
points: Mirror: left ↔ right; water: top ↔ bottom
Vertical-mirror-safe letters: A H I M O T U V W X Y
Water-safe letters: B C D E H I K O X
Series: one element at a time — rotation, count, shading, position
Embedded figure: same size and orientation
Check asymmetric letters to separate close options

chapters.title: Reasoning: cubes, dice & dot situation

cards.title: Painted cube cut into n × n × n small cubes
Dice
cards.body: On a standard die, opposite faces add up to **7** (1–6, 2–5, 3–4). For other dice, compare two positions that share a face: the faces that never appear together with a given face are often opposite to it.

cards.title: Dot situation
cards.body: A figure shows a dot inside some overlapping shapes (e.g. inside the circle and square but outside the triangle). Pick the option where you can place a dot in a region that is inside exactly the same shapes and outside the same others.

cards.title: Paper folding and cutting
cards.body: Unfold step by step in reverse order. Every cut or punch is reflected across each fold line, so one hole in paper folded twice usually becomes four holes, placed symmetrically.

cards.title: Painted cube
cards.body: A 4 × 4 × 4 painted cube is cut into 64 unit cubes. Two faces painted = 12 × (4 − 2) = **24**. No face painted = (4 − 2)³ = **8**. Check: 8 + 24 + 24 + 8 = 64.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Write the four cube formulas on your rough sheet before starting the section. In dot-situation questions, list the shapes for the dot first ('in circle + square, not triangle') before opening the options.

cards.q: A 4 × 4 × 4 painted cube is cut into unit cubes. How many have exactly two faces painted?
On a standard die, which number is opposite 2?
cards.explain: Opposite faces of a standard die sum to 7, so 2 is opposite 5.

cards.q: In the same 4 × 4 × 4 cube, how many small cubes have no painted face?

notes.p: A cube painted on all faces is cut into n × n × n small cubes. Every small cube belongs to exactly one group:
points: Two faces painted: 12(n − 2) (along the 12 edges, excluding corners)
One face painted: 6(n − 2)² (centre parts of the 6 faces)
No face painted: (n − 2)³ (the hidden inner cube)
Check: the four groups add up to n³

notes.p:
**Example 1.** n = 3 (27 small cubes).
Step 1: Three faces = 8; two faces = 12 × 1 = 12.
Step 2: One face = 6 × 1² = 6; none = 1³ = 1.
Check: 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = **27** ✓.

**Example 2.** n = 5 (125 small cubes).
Step 1: Two faces = 12 × 3 = **36**.
Step 2: One face = 6 × 3² = **54**.
Step 3: None = 3³ = **27**; corners = 8.
Check: 8 + 36 + 54 + 27 = 125 ✓.

**Cuts:** to cut a cube into 27 equal pieces you need 6 cuts (2 along each axis). In general, with a cuts, b cuts and c cuts along the three axes, pieces = (a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1).
On a **standard die**, opposite faces add to **7**: 1–6, 2–5, 3–4. For **non-standard dice** shown in two or more positions:
points: If two positions share one common face, the remaining faces in the same relative positions are opposite each other
Faces that appear together (adjacent) can never be opposite
If a number never appears with a given number, it is likely its opposite
Example: position 1 shows 1 with 2 and 3; position 2 shows 1 with 4 and 5. The only number never seen with 1 is 6, so 6 is opposite 1

notes.p:
A figure shows dots placed in regions of overlapping shapes (circle, square, triangle). You must find the option where a dot can be placed in a region with the **same membership**.

Method: (1) For each dot, write its condition — e.g. "inside circle and square, outside triangle". (2) In each option, look for a region satisfying **all** conditions for every dot. (3) Eliminate options quickly by checking the hardest condition first (usually the one inside three shapes).
